claim: Human Purkinje cells (PCs) are universally multi-branched.
source: While otherwise uncharacterized, human PCs are universally multi-branched.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by data presented in the manuscript showing that human PCs are almost exclusively multi-branched (Split or Poly morphologies).

claim: Human PCs have total dendritic lengths of 6–7 cm.
source: Human PCs are substantially larger than previously described; they exceed allometric constraint by cortical thickness and are the largest neuron in the brain with 6–7 cm total dendritic length.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by reconstruction data showing mean dendritic length of 63,645±4572 μm.

claim: Human PCs are the largest neuron in the brain.
source: Human PCs are substantially larger than previously described; they exceed allometric constraint by cortical thickness and are the largest neuron in the brain with 6–7 cm total dendritic length.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by comparison with pyramidal cells in the discussion showing human PCs (~65,000 μm) are substantially larger than pyramidal cells (~15,000 μm).

claim: Human PCs exceed allometric constraint by cortical thickness.
source: Human PCs are substantially larger than previously described; they exceed allometric constraint by cortical thickness and are the largest neuron in the brain with 6–7 cm total dendritic length.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data showing human PCs are ~4.5× wider than mouse PCs while only 2.3× taller, indicating horizontal expansion beyond what would be predicted by molecular layer thickness alone.

claim: Human PC spines are denser than mouse PC spines (6.9 vs 4.9 spines/μm).
source: Human spines are denser (6.9 vs 4.9 spines/μm), larger (~0.36 vs 0.29 μm), and include an unreported 'spine cluster' structure—features that may be congruent with enhanced PF association and amplification as human-specific adaptations.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by quantitative spine reconstruction data showing 6.81±0.77 vs 5.1±0.61 spines/μm.

claim: Human PC spines are larger than mouse PC spines (~0.36 vs 0.29 μm).
source: Human spines are denser (6.9 vs 4.9 spines/μm), larger (~0.36 vs 0.29 μm), and include an unreported 'spine cluster' structure—features that may be congruent with enhanced PF association and amplification as human-specific adaptations.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by spine head diameter measurements showing 0.36±0.1 μm vs 0.29±0.08 μm.

claim: Human PCs include an unreported 'spine cluster' structure not found in mouse.
source: Human spines are denser (6.9 vs 4.9 spines/μm), larger (~0.36 vs 0.29 μm), and include an unreported 'spine cluster' structure—features that may be congruent with enhanced PF association and amplification as human-specific adaptations.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by detailed characterization of spine clusters in human tissue with density of 0.52±0.16/μm, while only 1 of 1380 mouse spines met the criteria.

claim: Human PCs may receive 500,000 to 1 million synaptic inputs compared with 30–40,000 in mouse.
source: By extrapolation, human PCs may receive 500,000 to 1 million synaptic inputs compared with 30–40,000 in mouse.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and derived from combining measures of total dendritic length and spine density, with additional consideration of branched spines and spine clusters that may host multiple synapses.

claim: Multi-branched PCs are more prevalent in posterior and lateral cerebellum.
source: Multi-branched PCs are more prevalent in posterior and lateral cerebellum, co-varying with functional boundaries, supporting the hypothesis that this morphological motif permits expanded input multiplexing and may subserve task-dependent needs for input association.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by regional analysis showing increased prevalence of Poly PCs in Crus I/II compared to L5-6.

claim: Multi-branched PC prevalence co-varies with functional boundaries.
source: Multi-branched PCs are more prevalent in posterior and lateral cerebellum, co-varying with functional boundaries, supporting the hypothesis that this morphological motif permits expanded input multiplexing and may subserve task-dependent needs for input association.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by comparison of PC demographics with functional atlas data showing alignment between morphological classes and functional regions.

claim: Human PCs were substantially (~11×) longer than mouse PCs.
source: Human PCs were substantially (~11×) longer than in mouse, more than was previously appreciated (Kaneko et al., 2011; Louis et al., 2014; Masoli et al., 2024; Mavroudis et al., 2017; Mavroudis et al., 2022; Paula-Barbosa et al., 1980; Gao et al., 2011; Takeo et al., 2021; Joo et al., 2014; Figure 1C), having total dendritic lengths of 63,645±4572 μm and 6004±831 µm, respectively (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is directly stated in the results and supported by quantitative reconstruction data comparing human and mouse total dendritic length.

claim: Human PCs have total dendritic lengths of 63,645±4572 μm.
source: Human PCs were substantially (~11×) longer than in mouse, more than was previously appreciated (Kaneko et al., 2011; Louis et al., 2014; Masoli et al., 2024; Mavroudis et al., 2017; Mavroudis et al., 2022; Paula-Barbosa et al., 1980; Gao et al., 2011; Takeo et al., 2021; Joo et al., 2014; Figure 1C), having total dendritic lengths of 63,645±4572 μm and 6004±831 µm, respectively (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is directly stated in the results and supported by manual reconstruction data from n=5 human cells.

claim: Mouse PCs have total dendritic lengths of 6004±831 µm.

evidence: This is directly stated in the results and supported by manual reconstruction data from n=5 mouse cells.

claim: Human PCs had 3.9× the number of total branch segments compared to mouse (2750±247 vs 707±118).
source: Human PCs had 3.9× the number of total and terminal branch segments (2750±247 vs 707±118 and 1377±125 vs 355±59; Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: This is directly stated in the results and supported by quantitative reconstruction data.

claim: Human PCs had 3.9× the number of terminal branch segments compared to mouse (1377±125 vs 355±59).
source: Human PCs had 3.9× the number of total and terminal branch segments (2750±247 vs 707±118 and 1377±125 vs 355±59; Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: This is directly stated in the results and supported by quantitative reconstruction data.

claim: Human PC branching reached nearly double the maximum branch order compared to mouse (50±5.4 vs 28±5.3).
source: which were produced by branching that reached nearly double the maximum and average branch order (50±5.4 vs 28±5.3 and 25±2.5 vs 14±2.6; Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is directly stated in the results and supported by quantitative reconstruction data.

claim: Human PC branching reached nearly double the average branch order compared to mouse (25±2.5 vs 14±2.6).

evidence: This is directly stated in the results and supported by quantitative reconstruction data.

claim: Human primary dendrites commonly ramify parallel with the PC layer and bear numerous, often 7–8, compartments.
source: Despite considerable morphological variation, a trend emerged wherein human primary dendrites commonly ramified parallel with the PC layer and bore numerous, often 7–8 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), compartments that projected vertically toward the pial surface.
evidence: This is directly stated in the results and supported by morphological reconstruction data and quantification of primary dendrite compartments.

claim: Human PC arbors are ~4.5× wider than mouse PC arbors (644±126 μm vs 143±31 μm).
source: This alignment rendered their abor ~4.5× wider than in mouse (644±126 μm vs 143±31 μm; Figure 1G)
evidence: This is directly stated in the results and supported by quantitative reconstruction data measuring maximum arbor width.

claim: Human PC arbors are only 2.3× taller than mouse PC arbors (366±58 μm vs 158±22 μm).
source: while their molecular layer thickness—a crucial allometric variable—defined the maximal arbor height to be only 2.3× taller (366±58 μm vs 158±22 μm; Figure 1H).
evidence: This is directly stated in the results and supported by quantitative reconstruction data measuring maximum arbor height.

claim: Human PCs attained a horizontal dimensionality with 79±42% greater width than height.
source: Thus, human PCs attained a horizontal dimensionality with 79±42% greater width than height while mouse PCs had 6.3±31% greater height than width (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is directly stated in the results and supported by quantitative reconstruction data calculating the ratio of width to height.

claim: Mouse PCs had 6.3±31% greater height than width.
source: Thus, human PCs attained a horizontal dimensionality with 79±42% greater width than height while mouse PCs had 6.3±31% greater height than width (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is directly stated in the results and supported by quantitative reconstruction data calculating the ratio of width to height.

claim: Human branches ramified at more horizontal eccentricities than mouse branches (~37±24° vs 45±24°).
source: Across branching orders and somatic distances, human branches ramified at more horizontal eccentricities than in mouse (~37±24° vs 45±24°; Figure 1J).
evidence: This is directly stated in the results and supported by quantitative analysis of branch eccentricity relative to the PC layer.

claim: Both human and mouse dendrite eccentricities turned upward with increased distance from the soma.
source: Both human and mouse dendrite eccentricities turned upward with increased distance from the soma (~29±23°, 39±24°, 42±23° among branches in proximal, intermediate, and distal compartments vs 41±24°, 43±25°, and 51±23°; Figure 1J)
evidence: This is directly stated in the results and supported by quantitative analysis of branch eccentricity as a function of distance from soma.

claim: Human PC somata are 2× the diameter of mouse PC somata (32.8±3.07 μm vs 16.5±0.78 μm).
source: Emerging from a somatic compartment that is 2× the diameter (roughly 7.7× the volume) of mouse (32.8±3.07 μm vs 16.5±0.78 μm; Figure 1—figure supplement 2D)
evidence: This is directly stated in the results and supported by quantitative measurement of somatic diameter.

claim: Human PC somata are roughly 7.7× the volume of mouse PC somata.
source: Emerging from a somatic compartment that is 2× the diameter (roughly 7.7× the volume) of mouse (32.8±3.07 μm vs 16.5±0.78 μm; Figure 1—figure supplement 2D)
evidence: This is directly stated in the results and derived from the diameter measurements assuming spherical geometry.

claim: Human primary dendrites were 2.1× thicker than mouse primary dendrites (6.49±2.43 μm vs 3.12±1.17 μm).
source: human primary dendrites were 2.1× thicker (6.49±2.43 μm vs 3.12±1.17 μm; Figure 1K).
evidence: This is directly stated in the results and supported by quantitative measurement of primary dendrite diameter.

claim: Human dendrites narrow nearly tenfold as they branch.
source: Human dendrites narrow nearly tenfold as they branch (Figure 1L)
evidence: This is directly stated in the results and supported by quantitative analysis of dendrite diameter by branch order.

claim: The spiny dendrites of both human and mouse species converge on an apparently conserved thickness (~0.6–1 μm).
source: such that the spiny dendrites of both species converge on an apparently conserved thickness (~0.6–1 μm; Figure 1M, Figure 1—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is directly stated in the results and supported by quantitative analysis of dendrite diameter distributions.

claim: 95% of human dendritic length is devoted to thin, spiny dendrites with <1.3 μm diameter.

claim: 89% of mouse dendritic length is devoted to thin, spiny dendrites with <1.3 μm diameter.

source: Individual branch segments were 2.3× longer on average in human and varied more in their length (24.53±18.78 μm vs 9.23±5.7 μm; Figure 1P).

claim: Terminal dendritic segments were 3× longer in human than mouse (33.14±19.59 μm vs 10.9±5.81 μm).

claim: Human PCs exhibited higher spine density than mouse PCs (6.81±0.77 vs 5.1±0.61 spines/μm).

claim: Both human and mouse species had higher spine densities on distal dendrites.

claim: Increased PF input density on distal compartments may be a conserved mammalian trait.
source: Both species had higher densities on distal dendrites (6.32±0.62 to 7.1±0.77/μm in proximal vs distal compartments of human; 4.55±0.55 to 5.48±0.35/μm in mouse; Figure 2C), suggesting that increased PF input density on distal compartments may be a conserved mammalian trait (Kano et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the results as a suggestion based on the observed pattern in both species and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: A mouse PC has roughly 30–40,000 spines.
source: Combining measures of total dendritic length and spine density, we can extrapolate that a mouse PC has roughly 30–40,000 spines, consistent with recent findings (Nguyen et al., 2023)
evidence: This is stated in the results as an extrapolation from dendritic length and spine density measurements, and is consistent with cited recent findings.

claim: A human PC has roughly 400–600,000 spines.
source: Combining measures of total dendritic length and spine density, we can extrapolate that a mouse PC has roughly 30–40,000 spines, consistent with recent findings (Nguyen et al., 2023), while a human PC has roughly 400–600,000 spines.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an extrapolation from dendritic length and spine density measurements.

claim: At least 11% and possibly up to half of human PCs receive multiple CFs.
source: Thus, at least 11% and possibly up to half of human PCs receive multiple CFs, setting the minimum likelihood to the same rate (~15%) of multi-innervation observed in mouse (Busch and Hansel, 2023).

evidence: This is directly stated in the results and supported by classification of peripherin-labeled PCs by morphology and innervation pattern.

claim: Factors shaping the relationship between multi-branched structure and CF multi-innervation may be conserved across mice and humans.

evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference based on the observed correlation between multi-branched morphology and CF multi-innervation in both species.

claim: The population rate of CF multi-innervation may be at least 25% in human.

claim: Vermis largely resembled anterior hemisphere with an elevated rate of normative PCs and more Split than Poly PCs.

claim: The inter-hemisphere rate of PC subtypes varied more in Crus I/II than L5 and especially L6.

evidence: This is stated in the discussion and draws from cited transcriptomic studies.

evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citation.

claim: PC morphology and CF signaling is altered in disease models such as spinocerebellar ataxia.
source: In mouse, PC morphology and CF signaling is altered in disease models such as spinocerebellar ataxia (Du et al., 2013; Du et al., 2019) and syndromic autism (Simmons et al., 2022; Busch et al., 2023; Piochon et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to studies in mouse disease models.

claim: Human PC dendritic morphology was disrupted in essential tremor.
source: On the only occasions that human PC dendritic morphology has been measured with respect to cerebellar disease, it was disrupted in essential tremor (Louis et al., 2014; Mavroudis et al., 2022) and Friedreich's ataxia (Kemp et al., 2016)
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to studies in human disease.

claim: Human PC dendritic morphology was disrupted in Friedreich's ataxia.
source: On the only occasions that human PC dendritic morphology has been measured with respect to cerebellar disease, it was disrupted in essential tremor (Louis et al., 2014; Mavroudis et al., 2022) and Friedreich's ataxia (Kemp et al., 2016)
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citation.

claim: Dendritic abnormalities were recently reported in spinocerebellar ataxias and other neurodegenerative movement disorders.
source: and dendritic abnormalities were recently reported in spinocerebellar ataxias and other neurodegenerative movement disorders (Louis et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citation.

claim: The diameter of thin caliber dendrites is identical between human and mouse, indicating a shared constraint on dendritic thickness.
source: The diameter of thin caliber dendrites is identical, indicating a shared constraint on dendritic thickness, perhaps by limits of physiological conduction.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the observed data showing convergence of spiny dendrite diameter.

claim: Human and mouse PCs share similar fractal branching patterns.
source: We observed similar fractal branching patterns and relative average distances of peak branch number and dendritic length from the soma, suggesting a possible shared dependence on cell-autonomous factors governing the branching pattern.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the observed data on branching patterns.

claim: The confluence of invariant, allometric, and non-allometric morphological features may indicate that human PC physiology diverges from the rodent not only as a matter of scale but as a matter of kind.
source: While this cannot currently be tested directly, the confluence of invariant, allometric, and non-allometric morphological features may indicate that human PC physiology diverges from the rodent not only as a matter of scale (Masoli et al., 2024) but as a matter of kind.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a hypothesis based on the observed morphological differences.

claim: Spine clusters may be potentially fertile ground to explore new modes of synaptic and dendritic signaling.
source: Spine clusters may be potentially fertile ground to explore new modes of synaptic and dendritic signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as speculation about the functional significance of spine clusters.

claim: Spine clusters may operate as an associative structure and a new form of amplifying structure providing the substrate to initiate dendritic calcium spikes.
source: These two features may combine to produce both an associative structure, like proposed for branched spines (Loschky et al., 2022), and a new form of amplifying structure providing the substrate to initiate dendritic calcium spikes (Roome and Kuhn, 2018; Eilers et al., 1995; Hartell, 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as speculation about the functional properties of spine clusters, supported by citations to related phenomena.

claim: Human PCs may receive disproportionately more inputs than rodent PCs.
source: In addition to spine clusters, human PCs are more spine dense and thus may receive disproportionately more inputs than rodent PCs.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an inference from the observed higher spine density in human.

claim: The previously reported average human PC dendritic length was 10–20,000 μm.
source: The previously reported average human PC dendritic length was 10–20,000 μm, varying with methodology (Golgi impregnation [Louis et al., 2014; Paula-Barbosa et al., 1980] vs post-fix dye electroporation [Masoli et al., 2024]).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Previous knowledge would conclude that human PCs are the same size as pyramidal cells.
source: Our current knowledge, then, would conclude that human PCs are the same size as pyramidal cells (L2/3 are ~14,500 μm, <22,000 μm [Mohan et al., 2015]; thick tufted L5/6 are ~1–2000 μm longer [Mohan et al., 2015]; hippocampal CA1 are ~18,600 μm, <27,000 μm [Mertens et al., 2024]).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of what previous data would suggest, supported by citations.

claim: PCs are substantially bigger than pyramidal cells and boast the largest dendritic arbor of any recorded neuron in the human brain.
source: On the contrary, we demonstrate for the first time that PCs are substantially bigger than pyramidal cells and boast the largest dendritic arbor of any recorded neuron in the human brain.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the current study's reconstruction data showing ~65,000 μm dendritic length compared to ~15,000 μm for pyramidal cells.

claim: Pyramidal and PCs scale differently in mouse (~5500 vs ~6000 μm) than human (~15,000 vs ~65,000 μm).
source: Intriguingly, our findings also indicate that pyramidal and PCs scale differently in mouse (~5500 vs ~6000 μm) than human (~15,000 vs ~65,000 μm).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by comparison of the current study's data with cited pyramidal cell data.

claim: The human may receive ~750,000 synaptic inputs on spines.
source: As such, the human may receive ~750,000 synaptic inputs on spines.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an extrapolation accounting for branched spines and spine clusters that may host multiple synapses.

claim: The species' dendritic length ratio (11:1) belies an input ratio around 30:1.
source: It is not only staggering to consider a single neuron receiving ~1 million inputs, but it highlights that the species' dendritic length ratio (11:1) belies an input ratio around 30:1.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an inference from the combined effects of dendritic length, spine density, and spine cluster differences.

claim: Multi-branched structure permits CF multi-innervation by providing segregated synaptic territories where multiple CFs could avoid competitive pruning.
source: We predicted that multi-branched structure permits CF multi-innervation by providing segregated synaptic territories where multiple CFs could avoid the competitive pruning that would have prevented their translocation from soma to dendrite.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a hypothesis based on previous findings and supported by the current observations.

claim: The disproportionate width of human PCs may sample more distinct PF representations.
source: If conserved, spatial-functional PF clustering reported in mouse (Wilms and Häusser, 2015) would make their functional similarity diminish with distance. Thus, the disproportionate width of human PCs may sample more distinct PF representations.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as speculation based on the observed horizontal expansion and cited PF clustering in mouse.

claim: Human PCs likely perform highly complex input multiplexing and dendritic computations that are unlike what is commonly reported in mouse.
source: Taken together, human PCs likely perform highly complex input multiplexing and dendritic computations that are unlike what is commonly reported in mouse.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an inference from the combined morphological and input arrangement differences.

claim: CF multi-innervation may be an adaptation to maintain receptive field matching in multi-branched PCs with more disparate PF representations across segregated dendritic compartments.
source: We previously suggested that CF multi-innervation may be an adaptation to maintain receptive field matching in multi-branched PCs with more disparate PF representations across segregated dendritic compartments (Busch and Hansel, 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a hypothesis from previous work.

claim: Human PC output may convey more features of sensory, internal, or cognitive state.
source: As a possible consequence, human PC output may convey more features of sensory, internal, or cognitive state.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as speculation about the functional consequences of enhanced input multiplexing.

claim: Multi-branched PC computation may resemble mixed selectivity encoding by pyramidal cells involved in complex decision-making.
source: Thus, multi-branched PC computation may resemble mixed selectivity encoding by pyramidal cells involved in complex decision-making (Tye et al., 2024).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as speculation supported by citation to related phenomena in pyramidal cells.

claim: Expansion of input numerosity or strength does not necessarily improve computational capacity.
source: Importantly, expansion of input numerosity or strength does not necessarily improve computational capacity.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a cautionary note supported by examples from disease models.

claim: Excess CF innervation is linked to cellular and behavioral sensory over-responsiveness in mouse autism models.
source: Excess CF innervation is linked to cellular and behavioral sensory over-responsiveness in mouse autism models (Simmons et al., 2022; Busch et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations.

claim: Human essential tremor is characterized in part by excess CF innervation from ectopic lateral crossings.
source: Human essential tremor is characterized in part by excess CF innervation from ectopic lateral crossings (Wu et al., 2021) and translocation to thin dendrites (Pan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations.

claim: The relative proportions of multi-dendritic structure and horizontal orientation act as complementary toggles to generate four classes of morphological demography.
source: We propose that the relative proportions of multi-dendritic structure and horizontal orientation act as complementary toggles to generate four classes of morphological demography.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a proposed framework based on the observed regional patterns.

claim: The regional borders of each morphological class align well with four functional classes from a new consensus atlas of human cerebellum.
source: Surprisingly, the regional borders of each class align well with four functional classes from a new consensus atlas of human cerebellum (Nettekoven et al., 2024; Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by comparison with a cited functional atlas.

claim: Regions with more complex morphology roughly match regions processing information that is more cognitive and associative in nature.
source: Furthermore, regions with more complex morphology (increased multi-branched and horizontal orientation) roughly match regions processing information that is more cognitive (co-active with non-primary sensory neocortical regions) and associative (requiring integration and association of multi-modal inputs) in nature (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by comparison with functional data.

claim: The spatial scale of clustering and the comparative scale ratio are congruent with the absolute and relative widths of the dendritic arbor.
source: The spatial scale of clustering and the comparative scale ratio (~5–7× longer in human; enhanced clustering in core regions of 2 mm vs 400 μm) are congruent with the absolute and relative widths of the dendritic arbor.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the clustering data in relation to dendritic morphology.

claim: The clustering scale ratio exceeds the comparative PC height ratio.
source: Notably, the clustering scale ratio exceeds the comparative PC height ratio (a proxy for allometric constraint).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an observation supporting the idea that clustering is related to horizontal dendritic expansion.

claim: Cerebellar cortical region may employ 'patches' of homogeneous PC morphologies to create niches for heterogeneous computations.
source: This suggests that cerebellar cortical region, especially in human, may employ 'patches' of homogeneous PC morphologies to create niches for heterogeneous computations.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a hypothesis based on the observed clustering patterns.

claim: Nonrandom spatial clustering of neuronal cells by morphological subtype has not previously been described in other brain areas.
source: Nonrandom spatial clustering of neuronal cells by morphological subtype has not previously been described in other brain areas, potentially making this a cerebellum-specific means to boost functional diversity.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a claim about the novelty of the finding.

claim: PC dendrites are optimized to integrate the vast cerebellar input array and drive the sole cortical output.
source: Purkinje cell (PC) dendrites are optimized to integrate the vast cerebellar input array and drive the sole cortical output.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about PC function.

claim: PCs are classically seen as stereotypical computational units.
source: PCs are classically seen as stereotypical computational units
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a classical view in the field.

claim: Mouse PCs are morphologically diverse.
source: yet mouse PCs are morphologically diverse
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Mouse PCs with multi-branched structure can receive non-canonical climbing fiber multi-innervation that confers independent compartment-specific signaling.
source: and those with multi-branched structure can receive non-canonical climbing fiber (CF) multi-innervation that confers independent compartment-specific signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by previous work cited in the introduction.

claim: Being the sole output of the cerebellar cortex, Purkinje cells perform the final step to integrate all cortical input.
source: Being the sole output of the cerebellar cortex, Purkinje cells (PCs) perform the final step to integrate all cortical input.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about PC function.

claim: The dendritic arbor of each PC is the target of tens of thousands of granule cell parallel fiber axons.
source: The dendritic arbor of each PC is the target of tens of thousands of granule cell parallel fiber (PF) axons, which deliver an expansion recoding of mossy fiber contextual input (Albus, 1971; Marr, 1969)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to foundational theories.

claim: PCs receive prediction-error signals carried by one—or several—climbing fiber axons from the inferior olive.
source: and prediction-error signals carried by one—or several—climbing fiber (CF) axons from the inferior olive (Ito and Kano, 1982; Busch and Hansel, 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: PC dendrites are morphologically diverse.
source: Recent work has shown that PC dendrites are morphologically diverse (Busch and Hansel, 2023; Kaneko et al., 2011; Nedelescu et al., 2018)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: PC dendrite sub-branches can exhibit heterogeneous physiological excitability.
source: and their sub-branches can exhibit heterogeneous physiological excitability (Zang et al., 2018; Midtgaard, 1995; Ohtsuki, 2020; Ohtsuki et al., 2012; Roome and Kuhn, 2018; Zang and De Schutter, 2021; Cirtala and De Schutter, 2024).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Primary dendrite morphology can influence patterns of CF innervation.
source: Primary dendrite morphology can influence patterns of CF innervation, in some cases permitting non-canonical CF multi-innervation in adult mice that confers independent signaling across compartments in vivo (Busch and Hansel, 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: Dendritic compartments can undergo independent plasticity.
source: A study using patch-clamp electrophysiology in cerebellar slices found that dendritic compartments can undergo independent plasticity (Ohtsuki et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: Intrinsic and synaptic plasticity mechanisms can operate on distinct, compartment-level spatial scales to tune dendritic signaling.
source: Combined physiological and calcium imaging experiments in awake mice found that intrinsic and synaptic plasticity mechanisms can operate on distinct, compartment-level spatial scales to tune dendritic signaling and gate its impact on axosomatic output (Lin et al., 2024).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: Very little is known about the nature of human PC dendrite morphology, input arrangement, or physiology.
source: While this insight comes largely from the use of the experimentally accessible rodent cerebellum, human PCs are far more enigmatic. Very little is known about the nature of their dendrite morphology, input arrangement, or physiology.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a knowledge gap.

claim: The morphology of human PC dendrites have only been analyzed occasionally and in small numbers since their illustration by Golgi, 1874, and Ramón y Cajal, 1909.
source: Since their illustration by Golgi, 1874, and Ramón y Cajal, 1909, the morphology of human PC dendrites have only been analyzed occasionally and in small numbers (Eccles et al., 1967; Kato et al., 1985; Louis et al., 2014), eluding systematic quantification.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to historical work.

claim: Human PCs are almost universally multi-branched whereas a plurality of mouse PCs are Normative.
source: This approach revealed that human PCs are almost universally multi-branched whereas a plurality of mouse PCs are Normative.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction summarizing previous findings.

claim: In mice, ~25% of multi-branched PCs received multiple functionally distinct CFs while Normative cells did not.
source: In mice, ~25% of multi-branched PCs received multiple functionally distinct CFs while Normative cells did not, indicating a link between primary dendrite morphology and cellular physiology.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction summarizing previous findings.

claim: Recent work leveraged limited access to acute human cerebellar tissue and a comparative modeling approach to make important progress on understanding human PC physiology.
source: Human PC physiology, on the other hand, remains largely inaccessible, but recent work leveraged limited access to acute human cerebellar tissue and a comparative modeling approach to make important progress (Masoli et al., 2024.)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: PCs far exceed pyramidal cells in having the largest dendritic arbor in the human brain.
source: Our reconstructions reveal that—with dendritic lengths of 6–7 cm—PCs far exceed pyramidal cells in having the largest dendritic arbor in the human brain.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by the reconstruction data presented in the results.

claim: Human cells have increased spine size (~0.36 vs 0.29 μm diameter) and density (6.9 vs 4.9 spines/μm)—receiving upward of 1 million inputs compared with 30–40,000 in mouse.
source: In support of this, we found that human cells have increased spine size (~0.36 vs 0.29 μm diameter) and density (6.9 vs 4.9 spines/μm)—receiving upward of 1 million inputs compared with 30–40,000 in mouse
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by the spine reconstruction data presented in the results.

claim: Human PCs host a previously unreported 'spine cluster' structure not found in mouse.
source: and host a previously unreported 'spine cluster' structure not found in mouse.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by the spine reconstruction data presented in the results.

claim: Non-canonical CF multi-innervation is present in adult human, as in mouse.
source: Co-labeling PCs (calbindin) and CFs (peripherin) confirms that non-canonical CF multi-innervation is present in adult human, as in mouse (Busch and Hansel, 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by the peripherin co-labeling data presented in the results.

claim: The regional prevalence of a multi-branched motif among PC populations covaries with human functional boundaries.
source: The regional prevalence of a multi-branched motif among PC populations covaries with human functional boundaries and exhibits subregional patches of clustered morphologies.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by the regional analysis data presented in the results.

claim: PC populations exhibit subregional patches of clustered morphologies.
source: The regional prevalence of a multi-branched motif among PC populations covaries with human functional boundaries and exhibits subregional patches of clustered morphologies.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by the clustering analysis data presented in the results.

claim: A multi-branched structure can provide for enhanced input multiplexing.
source: This supports the hypothesis that a multi-branched structure can provide for enhanced input multiplexing and that this may subserve complex multimodal association and learning in posterior and lateral cerebellar regions.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a hypothesis supported by the regional analysis.

claim: Enhanced input multiplexing may subserve complex multimodal association and learning in posterior and lateral cerebellar regions.
source: This supports the hypothesis that a multi-branched structure can provide for enhanced input multiplexing and that this may subserve complex multimodal association and learning in posterior and lateral cerebellar regions.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a hypothesis supported by the regional analysis.
